study.title: International atomic clock comparison achieving $5\times 10^{-18}$ uncertainty

cover.headline: Two atomic clocks 2,220 km apart **now agree to within a second every 6 billion years**.

slides.title: This early paper reports a milestone toward changing how the SI second is defined, using light instead of microwaves.
slides.body:
The test reached a fractional uncertainty below 5×10⁻¹⁸. The team says this is an important step toward an optical change to the SI second.

If the approach holds, timekeeping could shift from today's clocks to optical ones.

slides.title: The two clocks showed a fractional frequency difference of 1.0 plus or minus 4.8 times 10⁻¹⁸.
slides.body:
Both clocks use a single ytterbium ion. They were compared remotely via a 2,220 kilometre optical fibre link using over one million seconds of data.

The uncertainty was dominated by relativistic redshift correction between the two sites.

slides.title: Both clocks measure the same energy jump in a ytterbium ion, built independently by teams in the UK and Germany.
slides.body:
The energy jump is a specific shift between levels in the ion. Measuring its frequency gives an extremely stable tick.

The test also let the team search for violations of Lorentz invariance.

caveats: This is a preprint. It has not been peer reviewed, so no independent expert has checked the work yet.
The measurement uncertainty was dominated by relativistic redshift correction, which includes time-varying gravity potential differences between the two sites.
The clocks use a single ion species and one energy jump, so this does not yet confirm agreement across different optical clock designs.

source.abstract: Two single-ion optical clocks, located in the United Kingdom and in Germany, are compared remotely via a 2220\,km long optical fiber link. Both clocks are based on the ${}^2S_{1/2} (F=0)\leftrightarrow {}^2F_{7/2} (F=3)$ electric octupole (E3) transition in $^{171}\text{Yb}^+$. Using more than $10^6$ seconds of measurement data, we determine a fractional frequency difference of $1.0(4.8)\times 10^{-18}$, demonstrating agreement of the independently developed systems. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first international clock comparison reaching a fractional uncertainty below $5\times 10^{-18}$, an important milestone towards an anticipated optical redefinition of the SI second. The measurement uncertainty is dominated by that of the relativistic redshift correction between the two sites, which includes time-varying gravity potential differences. We exploit the large baseline between the two clocks to search for violations of Lorentz invariance. In the absence of statistically significant modulations, we improve constraints on the Robertson-Mansouri-Sexl parameter $α$ by approximately a factor of five in the uncertainty, and provide limits on corresponding parameters within the Standard-Model Extension framework.
